name: Vilvanatheswarar Temple, Thiruvalam
deity: Shiva as Vilvanatheswarar, lord of the bael tree, with the Goddess Vallambigai (Dhanumadhyambal)
period: A Paadal Petra Sthalam of Thondai Nadu, the Thiruvallam of the Tevaram, sung by Sambandar (7th century); Pallava, Bana and Chola inscriptions
dynasty: Pallava, Bana and Chola, with a largely Nayak-period structure
summary: By the Niva river near Vellore, where tradition says Ganesha circled his parents to win the fruit, Shiva reigns as Vilvanatheswarar in a temple whose walls carry inscriptions from the Pallava age onward.

sections.history: Thiruvalam is a village of Vellore district on the Niva river, also called the Ponnai. Its temple to Shiva as Vilvanatheswarar is one of the 276 Paadal Petra Sthalams and a Paadal Petra Sthalam of Thondai Nadu, sung by Sambandar, who knew the place as Thiruvallam. Few shrines of the region hold so long a written record: its walls carry inscriptions from the time of the Pallava king Nandivarman II in the eighth century and then of the Cholas — Rajaraja I, Rajendra I and Kulottunga I and III among them. The Bana chiefs, vassals of the great dynasties, are named here too, and historians have read Thiruvalam as one of their seats. Many parts of the complex are of Chola date, while much of the present masonry belongs to the Nayak period of the sixteenth century.
sections.architecture: The temple is entered through a five-tiered gopuram, and its shrines are enclosed within concentric rectangular walls of granite. The sanctum of Vilvanatheswarar rises under a three-tiered vimana, and the Goddess Vallambigai has her own shrine. Within the enclosures stand shrines to Ganesha — honoured here for the story that gave the village its name — to Murugan, to Vishwanatha and to Gajalakshmi, and more than one Nandi keeps watch over the Lord.
sections.legends: The village takes its name from the most familiar of the stories of Shiva's sons. Shiva held out a single fruit to whichever son first went around the world. Murugan set off on his peacock; Ganesha, with only his mouse to ride, walked around his parents, Shiva and Parvati, saying that they were his whole world, and won the fruit. Tradition holds that he made that round — valam in Tamil — here, and so the place became Thiruvalam. The river has its own story: Shiva called to it, 'Nee va' — 'you, come' — and it turned its course towards the temple, taking the name Niva.
sections.festivals: The ten-day Brahmotsavam in the Tamil month of Masi (February–March) is the temple's principal festival. Pradosham, Maha Shivaratri, Karthigai Deepam and the festivals of Ganesha are also observed with devotion; confirm dates locally.
sections.experience: Thiruvalam rewards an unhurried visit: the devotee can worship the Lord of the bael tree, pause at the shrine of the Ganesha whose round named the village, and walk the granite enclosures reading, if one has the eye for it, centuries of gifts carved into the walls. The temple is easily joined to a visit to Vellore and Katpadi nearby.

visit.timings: Open daily in morning and evening sessions with a midday closure. Confirm current timings locally before visiting.
visit.dressCode: Modest traditional dress is expected — shoulders and knees covered; footwear is left outside before entering. Follow the posted rules and the priests' guidance.
visit.photography: Photography is not permitted inside the sanctum; in the outer corridors, ask the temple staff before taking pictures, especially of rituals and the festival bronzes.
visit.gettingThere: Thiruvalam lies about 15 km east of Vellore, between Katpadi and Ranipet, and has a small railway station on the Chennai–Katpadi line. Katpadi Junction is the nearest major railhead, buses run from Vellore and Katpadi, and Chennai International Airport is the nearest major airport.
